subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Iranian Tea Culture
description: A short lesson to help you apply Iranian Tea Culture.

hook.text: In Iran, tea is served with a sugar cube (nabat) held between the teeth—you sip through the dissolving crystal.

buildup.text: Iranian tea is brewed in a samovar—a heated urn borrowed from Russian tradition, now central to Iranian homes.

discovery.text: Chaikhanehs (tea houses) are gathering spots for men to play backgammon, smoke hookah, and discuss politics.

twist.text: Iran grows tea in the northern Gilan province. Despite being a desert country, its Caspian coast is lush and humid.

climax.text: Tea replaced coffee as Iran's drink in the 19th century when overland trade routes from India made tea more accessible.

punchline.text: Sugar on the teeth, tea through the crystal. Iran made sipping an art.

quiz.question: How is sugar traditionally consumed with Iranian tea?
options: Held as a cube between the teeth and sipped through

details.summary: Iran is one of the world's heaviest tea-consuming countries, with tea deeply embedded in daily social and business life. Tea is brewed strong in a samovar and served in small glass cups called estekans. Sugar is traditionally held between the teeth while sipping, a method called ghand-pahlu.
details.whyItMatters: Iranian tea culture blends Russian samovar traditions with Central Asian hospitality customs, creating a unique and pervasive tea culture that defines daily Iranian life.
takeaways: Tea is deeply embedded in all Iranian social and business life
It is brewed in a samovar and served in small glass estekans
Sugar is traditionally held between the teeth while sipping

faq.question: What is the ghand-pahlu method of drinking tea?
faq.answer: Ghand-pahlu means placing a sugar cube or piece of rock candy between the teeth and sipping hot tea through it. The sugar dissolves slowly, sweetening each sip naturally. It is an older tradition still practiced by many Iranians, though adding sugar directly to the cup is also common.

faq.question: When do Iranians drink tea?
faq.answer: Constantly. Tea accompanies breakfast, follows every meal, is served at all business meetings, and flows freely at social gatherings. It is the first thing offered to any guest. A traditional Iranian home always has a samovar ready. Tea consumption is estimated at over 100,000 tons annually.
